--- title: "Monte Carlo Methods in Inference 🧪" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Monte Carlo Methods in Inference

Lecture A: Monte Carlo estimation, standard errors, MSE, confidence levels

Lecture B: hypothesis testing review, Type I error, power, sample size, Count Five test

::: notes - Rizzo Chapter 7 plus the hypothesis-testing review notes (Chapt7-Hyp-Test). Lecture A ends after the empirical confidence level; Lecture B starts with the testing framework. ::: # Lecture A: Monte Carlo Methods for Estimation {#part-a} ## What Is a Monte Carlo Method in Inference? - Chapter 6 used simulation to compute **integrals**. Here we use simulation to study **statistical procedures**: + What is the bias / standard error / MSE of an estimator? + What is the true coverage of a confidence interval? + What is the Type I error rate or power of a test? + Which of two procedures is better, and when? - Parametric bootstrap flavor: we simulate from a **known** model, repeat the procedure many times, and summarize. ::: algo 1. For $j = 1,\dots,m$: generate a sample $x^{(j)}$ from the model; compute the statistic/decision $\hat\theta^{(j)}$. 2. Summarize the replicates $\hat\theta^{(1)},\dots,\hat\theta^{(m)}$ (mean, sd, proportion, quantiles). ::: ## Example 7.1: Basic Monte Carlo Estimation $X_1, X_2\iid N(0,1)$. Estimate $\theta = \E|X_1 - X_2|$ (exact value $2/\sqrt\pi$). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) m <- 1000 g <- numeric(m) for (i in 1:m) { x <- rnorm(2) g[i] <- abs(x[1] - x[2]) } est <- mean(g) c(estimate = est, exact = 2 / sqrt(pi), se = sqrt(sum((g - mean(g))^2)) / m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate exact se 1.13620 1.12838 0.02741 ``` ::: ::: - The standard error of a sample mean of $m$ replicates is $\widehat{\se} = \frac1m\sqrt{\sum_j(g_j - \bar g)^2}$. ## Example 7.2: MSE of a Trimmed Mean The $k$th level trimmed mean $\bar X_{[-k]} = \frac{1}{n-2k}\sum_{i=k+1}^{n-k}X_{(i)}$. Estimate its MSE when sampling from $N(0,1)$ ($\theta = 0$): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; m <- 1000; set.seed(4750) tmean <- numeric(m) for (i in 1:m) { x <- sort(rnorm(n)) tmean[i] <- sum(x[2:(n - 1)]) / (n - 2) } mse <- mean(tmean^2) c(mse = mse, se = sqrt(sum((tmean - mean(tmean))^2)) / m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mse se 0.052815 0.007264 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 7.3: Trimmed Mean Under Contamination Compare MSE for all trimming levels under $N(0,1)$ and the contaminated normal $0.9\,N(0,1) + 0.1\,N(0,100)$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(522); n <- 20; K <- n / 2 - 1; m <- 1000 mse <- matrix(0, n / 2, 6) trimmed.mse <- function(n, m, k, p) { tmean <- numeric(m) for (i in 1:m) { sigma <- sample(c(1, 10), size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(p, 1 - p)) x <- sort(rnorm(n, 0, sigma)) tmean[i] <- sum(x[(k + 1):(n - k)]) / (n - 2 * k) } mse.est <- mean(tmean^2); se.mse <- sqrt(mean((tmean - mean(tmean))^2)) / sqrt(m) c(mse.est, se.mse) } for (k in 0:K) { mse[k + 1, 1:2] <- trimmed.mse(n = n, m = m, k = k, p = 1.0) mse[k + 1, 3:4] <- trimmed.mse(n = n, m = m, k = k, p = .95) mse[k + 1, 5:6] <- trimmed.mse(n = n, m = m, k = k, p = .9) } matplot(0:K, n * mse[, c(1, 3, 5)], type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c(1, "#2E5BBA", "#C0392B"), xlab = "k (k = 9 is the median)", ylab = "n x MSE", log = "y") legend("topright", c("p = 1 (normal)", "p = .95", "p = .90"), col = c(1, "#2E5BBA", "#C0392B"), lwd = 2, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/13-mc-inference/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes - Under the normal model the untrimmed mean (k = 0) is best; under contamination moderate trimming wins by a lot. The median (k = 9) is a robust compromise. ::: ## Example 7.4: Confidence Interval for a Variance For a normal sample, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1)$, so a one-sided 95% **upper confidence limit** is $(n-1)S^2/\chi^2_\alpha$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; alpha <- .05; set.seed(4750) x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2) UCL <- (n - 1) * var(x) / qchisq(alpha, df = n - 1) UCL # should cover sigma^2 = 4 about 95% of the time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6.403 ``` ::: ::: ## Examples 7.5 - 7.6: Empirical Confidence Level ::: algo 1. For $j = 1,\dots,m$: generate a sample, compute the interval $C_j$, and set $y_j = I(\theta\in C_j)$. 2. The empirical confidence level is $\bar y = \frac1m\sum y_j$. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; alpha <- .05; set.seed(4750) calcCI <- function(n, alpha) { y <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2); (n - 1) * var(y) / qchisq(alpha, df = n - 1) } UCL <- replicate(1000, expr = calcCI(n = n, alpha = alpha)) mean(UCL > 4) # normal data: OK ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.953 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} UCL2 <- replicate(1000, expr = { x <- rchisq(n, df = 2); (n - 1) * var(x) / qchisq(alpha, df = n - 1) }) mean(UCL2 > 4) # chi^2(2) data, variance 4: badly below 95%! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.799 ``` ::: ::: ::: danger The $\chi^2$ interval for $\sigma^2$ is **not robust** to departures from normality. A $t$ interval for $\mu$ is much more robust (try it: Exercise 7.A). ::: # Lecture B: Monte Carlo Methods for Hypothesis Tests {#part-b} ## Hypothesis Testing: A General Framework Hypothesis testing is the most used methodology of statistics: 1. Build or assume a **statistical model** for the data. 2. Write the hypothesis of interest in terms of the **parameters** of the model. 3. Use a **decision rule** (that controls the rate of false discovery) to draw a conclusion. **Elements:** (1) null hypothesis $H_0$; (2) alternative (research) hypothesis $H_a$; (3) test statistic; (4) decision rule (rejection region); (5) conclusion. ## Example: The Courtroom - $H_0$: the person is innocent; $H_a$: the person is guilty - Test statistic: the evidence; decision rule: the jury's decision - Conclusion: "guilty" **or** "not enough evidence to convict" (never "innocent"!) ## Example: Does the Diet Work? 25 subjects on a new diet, 25 on placebo for eight weeks; count how many lost weight. | | Placebo | New diet | |---|---|---| | $n$ | 25 | 25 | | lost weight | 4 | 6 | $X_1\sim\text{Bin}(25,\pi_1)$, $X_2\sim\text{Bin}(25,\pi_2)$; $H_0:\pi_1 = \pi_2$ vs. $H_a:\pi_1 < \pi_2$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prop.test(c(6, 4), c(25, 25), alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)$p.value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2398 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fisher.test(matrix(c(6, 19, 4, 21), 2), alternative = "greater")$p.value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.3626 ``` ::: ::: ## Types of Error | | $H_0$ true | $H_a$ true | |---|---|---| | Reject $H_0$ | **Type I error** ($\alpha$) | correct (power $1-\beta$) | | Do not reject $H_0$ | correct | **Type II error** ($\beta$) | - $\alpha = P(\text{falsely reject } H_0)$, chosen beforehand (0.10, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001). - $\beta = P(\text{falsely accept } H_0)$ can be very large. - We cannot make both small with a fixed $n$; too small an $\alpha$ means no discoveries. ## Testing a Mean: The $z$ Test $$ z = \frac{\bar y - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\qquad \begin{cases} H_a:\mu>\mu_0: & \text{reject if } z > z_\alpha\\ H_a:\mu<\mu_0: & \text{reject if } z < -z_\alpha\\ H_a:\mu\neq\mu_0: & \text{reject if } |z| > z_{\alpha/2} \end{cases} $$ Assumes $\sigma$ known and $n\ge 30$ or a normal population. **Blood pressure:** $n = 100$, $\bar y = 121.5$, $\sigma = 5$, $H_0:\mu = 120$ vs $H_a:\mu > 120$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- (121.5 - 120) / (5 / sqrt(100)); c(z = z, critical = qnorm(.95), p_value = 1 - pnorm(z)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z critical p_value 3.00000 1.64485 0.00135 ``` ::: ::: **Anti-bacterial soap:** $n = 35$, $\bar y = 31.2$, $s = 8.4$, $H_0:\mu = 33$ vs $H_a:\mu<33$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- (31.2 - 33) / (8.4 / sqrt(35)); c(z = z, critical = -qnorm(.95), p_value = pnorm(z)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` z critical p_value -1.2677 -1.6449 0.1024 ``` ::: ::: ::: question We failed to reject. Can we conclude that the soap is **not** effective? Why not? ::: ## Example 7.7: Empirical Type I Error Rate $X_1,\dots,X_{20}\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$; test $H_0:\mu = 500$ vs. $H_1:\mu>500$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ with $T^* = (\bar X - 500)/(S/\sqrt{20})\sim t(19)$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; alpha <- .05; mu0 <- 500; sigma <- 100 m <- 10000; p <- numeric(m); set.seed(4750) for (j in 1:m) { x <- rnorm(n, mu0, sigma) ttest <- t.test(x, alternative = "greater", mu = mu0) p[j] <- ttest$p.value } p.hat <- mean(p < alpha) se.hat <- sqrt(p.hat * (1 - p.hat) / m) c(p.hat, se.hat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.05400 0.00226 ``` ::: ::: - The empirical Type I error rate should be within about $2\sqrt{\alpha(1-\alpha)/m}$ of $\alpha$. ## Is the $t$ Test Robust? Type I Error Under Skewed Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); m <- 5000 sapply(c(normal = "norm", exponential = "exp", lognormal = "lnorm"), function(dist) { mean(replicate(m, { x <- switch(dist, norm = rnorm(20, 1), exp = rexp(20, 1), lnorm = rlnorm(20, 0, 1) / exp(.5)) t.test(x, mu = 1, alternative = "greater")$p.value < .05 })) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` normal exponential lognormal 0.0570 0.0168 0.0100 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - All three populations have mean 1. The one-sided t test is conservative for right-skewed data in the upper tail here; check the lower-tail test too. ::: ## Example 7.8: Skewness Test of Normality $$ \sqrt{b_1} = \frac{\frac1n\sum(X_i - \bar X)^3}{\left(\frac1n\sum(X_i-\bar X)^2\right)^{3/2}},\qquad \sqrt{b_1}\approx N\!\left(0, \frac6n\right) \text{ under normality.} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sk <- function(x) { xbar <- mean(x); m3 <- mean((x - xbar)^3); m2 <- mean((x - xbar)^2); m3 / m2^1.5 } n <- c(10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500) cv <- qnorm(.975, 0, sqrt(6 / n)) # asymptotic critical values cv.exact <- qnorm(.975, 0, sqrt(6 * (n - 2) / ((n + 1) * (n + 3)))) # using the finite-sample variance p.reject <- p.reject.exact <- numeric(length(n)); m <- 10000; set.seed(4750) for (i in 1:length(n)) { sktests <- replicate(m, sk(rnorm(n[i]))) p.reject[i] <- mean(abs(sktests) >= cv[i]) p.reject.exact[i] <- mean(abs(sktests) >= cv.exact[i]) } rbind(n, asymptotic = p.reject, finite_sample = p.reject.exact) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] n 10.0000 20.0000 30.0000 50.0000 100.0000 500.0000 asymptotic 0.0120 0.0267 0.0349 0.0413 0.0476 0.0463 finite_sample 0.0527 0.0529 0.0532 0.0517 0.0530 0.0477 ``` ::: ::: ## Power of a Test $$ \pi(\theta) = P_\theta(\text{reject } H_0),\qquad \text{power at } \theta_1\in\Theta_1 = 1 - \beta(\theta_1). $$ What increases power? Smaller $\sigma$; $\mu_a$ farther from $\mu_0$; **larger $n$**; larger $\alpha$. ::: algo **Empirical power** at $\theta_1$: for $j = 1,\dots,m$, generate a sample under $\theta = \theta_1$, perform the test, record $I_j = 1$ if $H_0$ is rejected. Then $\hat\pi(\theta_1) = \bar I$, with $\widehat{\se} = \sqrt{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)/m}$. ::: ## Example 7.9: Empirical Power of the $t$ Test ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; m <- 1000; mu0 <- 500; sigma <- 100 mu <- c(seq(450, 650, 10)); M <- length(mu) power <- numeric(M); set.seed(4750) for (i in 1:M) { pvalues <- replicate(m, expr = { x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu[i], sd = sigma) t.test(x, alternative = "greater", mu = mu0)$p.value }) power[i] <- mean(pvalues <= .05) } se <- sqrt(power * (1 - power) / m) plot(mu, power, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(pi(theta))) arrows(mu, power - 2 * se, mu, power + 2 * se, angle = 90, code = 3, length = .03) abline(v = mu0, lty = 3); abline(h = .05, lty = 3) lines(mu, 1 - pt(qt(.95, n - 1), n - 1, ncp = (mu - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))), col = "red", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/13-mc-inference/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The red curve is the exact power from the noncentral $t$ distribution. ## Choosing the Sample Size To detect $\Delta = |\mu_a - \mu_0|$ with power $1-\beta$ at level $\alpha$ ($\sigma$ known): $$ \text{one-sided: } n = \sigma^2\frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2}{\Delta^2},\qquad \text{two-sided: } n = \sigma^2\frac{(z_{\alpha/2}+z_\beta)^2}{\Delta^2}. $$ **Cereal boxes.** Labeled 16 oz, filled with mean 16.37 oz, $\sigma = 0.225$. Test $H_0:\mu = 16.37$ vs $H_a:\mu<16.37$ at $\alpha = .05$. How many boxes to detect $\mu\le 16.27$ with power 0.99? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n_req <- 0.225^2 * (qnorm(.95) + qnorm(.99))^2 / 0.10^2 c(n = n_req, rounded_up = ceiling(n_req)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n rounded_up 79.84 80.00 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} power.t.test(delta = 0.10, sd = 0.225, power = 0.99, type = "one.sample", alternative = "one.sided")$n ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 81.21 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) # check by simulation at n = 80 mean(replicate(10000, { y <- rnorm(80, 16.27, .225); (mean(y) - 16.37) / (.225 / sqrt(80)) < -qnorm(.95) })) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9868 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 7.10: Power of the Skewness Test Against the contaminated normal $(1-\varepsilon)N(0,1) + \varepsilon N(0,100)$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} alpha <- .1; n <- 30; m <- 2500 epsilon <- c(seq(0, .15, .01), seq(.15, 1, .05)); N <- length(epsilon) pwr <- numeric(N); cv <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2, 0, sqrt(6 * (n - 2) / ((n + 1) * (n + 3)))) set.seed(4750) for (j in 1:N) { e <- epsilon[j] sktests <- replicate(m, { sigma <- sample(c(1, 10), replace = TRUE, size = n, prob = c(1 - e, e)) as.integer(abs(sk(rnorm(n, 0, sigma))) >= cv) }) pwr[j] <- mean(sktests) } plot(epsilon, pwr, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = bquote(epsilon), ylim = c(0, 1), ylab = "power") abline(h = .1, lty = 3); se <- sqrt(pwr * (1 - pwr) / m) lines(epsilon, pwr + 2 * se, lty = 3); lines(epsilon, pwr - 2 * se, lty = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/13-mc-inference/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 7.11: Comparing Tests of Normality Compare the skewness test with Shapiro-Wilk (`shapiro.test`) and the energy test (`energy::mvnorm.etest`). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} alpha <- .1; n <- 30; m <- 1000; eps <- c(0, .05, .1, .2, .5) set.seed(4750) res <- sapply(eps, function(e) { r <- replicate(m, { x <- rnorm(n, 0, sample(c(1, 10), replace = TRUE, size = n, prob = c(1 - e, e))) c(skewness = abs(sk(x)) >= cv, shapiro = shapiro.test(x)$p.value <= alpha) }) rowMeans(r) }) colnames(res) <- paste0("eps=", eps); round(res, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` eps=0 eps=0.05 eps=0.1 eps=0.2 eps=0.5 skewness 0.091 0.644 0.806 0.810 0.435 shapiro 0.093 0.667 0.896 0.986 0.909 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip With `energy` installed, add `energy::mvnorm.etest(x, R = 200)$p.value <= alpha`: it is the most powerful of the three for this alternative (and costly, since it uses a bootstrap). ::: ## Application: The "Count Five" Test (Examples 7.12 - 7.16) McGrath and Yeh (2005): to compare the **spread** of two samples, count the number of *extreme points* of each sample relative to the range of the other. Declare unequal variance if either count exceeds **five**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) x1 <- rnorm(20, 0, sd = 1); x2 <- rnorm(20, 0, sd = 1.5) y <- c(x1, x2); group <- rep(1:2, each = length(x1)) par(mar = c(2, 4, 1, 1)); boxplot(y ~ group, boxwex = .3, xlim = c(.5, 2.5), horizontal = TRUE); points(y, group) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/13-mc-inference/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} out1 <- sum(x1 > max(x2)) + sum(x1 < min(x2)); out2 <- sum(x2 > max(x1)) + sum(x2 < min(x1)) c(out1 = out1, out2 = out2, max = max(out1, out2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` out1 out2 max 0 8 8 ``` ::: ::: ## Examples 7.14 - 7.16: Size and Power of Count Five ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} count5test <- function(x, y) { X <- x - mean(x); Y <- y - mean(y) outx <- sum(X > max(Y)) + sum(X < min(Y)) outy <- sum(Y > max(X)) + sum(Y < min(X)) return(as.integer(max(c(outx, outy)) > 5)) # return 1 (reject) or 0 (do not reject H0) } set.seed(4750); m <- 10000 size_equal_n <- mean(replicate(m, count5test(rnorm(20), rnorm(20)))) size_unequal_n <- mean(replicate(m, count5test(rnorm(20), rnorm(50)))) power_sd1.5 <- mean(replicate(m, count5test(rnorm(20, 0, 1), rnorm(20, 0, 1.5)))) c(size_equal_n = size_equal_n, size_unequal_n = size_unequal_n, power_sd1.5 = power_sd1.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` size_equal_n size_unequal_n power_sd1.5 0.0541 0.2919 0.3249 ``` ::: ::: ::: danger With unequal sample sizes the Count Five test does **not** control the Type I error rate at 0.0625. Monte Carlo reveals this immediately; a fix is a permutation version (Ch 10). ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Monte Carlo estimation: replicate the procedure, summarize, and **report the Monte Carlo SE**. - Empirical confidence level and Type I error rate check whether a procedure keeps its promises. - Empirical power curves compare tests and choose sample sizes. - Robustness: the $t$ test for $\mu$ is fairly robust; the $\chi^2$ interval for $\sigma^2$ is not. ::: ::: your-turn Estimate the power of the $t$ test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (`wilcox.test`) for $n = 20$ when the data are $t(3)$-distributed with location $\theta\in[0, 1.5]$. Which test would you recommend? :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
